questions.question: In an auction of a single object, what makes bidder $i$'s valuation $\theta_i$ a private value?
options: Only $i$ knows $\theta_i$, and the other bidders' information would not change it.
Only $i$ knows $\theta_i$, though the others' information could still change it.
Every bidder knows $\theta_i$, but nobody else would value the object the same way.
$\theta_i$ differs from every other bidder's valuation of the object.

questions.question: One object is sold to $n$ bidders; bidder $i$ privately knows her valuation $\theta_i$ and gets $\theta_i-p_i$ if she wins, $-p_i$ if she loses ($p_i$: her payment). Two bidders happen to have exactly the same valuation, $\theta_1=\theta_2$. Can the values still be private?
options: No: private values must differ, otherwise the bidders share a common value.
No: when values coincide each bidder can infer the other's value from her own.
Yes: equal values can still each be a personal valuation known only to its owner.
Yes, but only if each bidder also knows that the other's value equals her own.

questions.question: One object is sold to $n$ bidders; bidder $i$ privately knows her valuation $\theta_i$ and gets $\theta_i-p_i$ if she wins, $-p_i$ if she loses ($p_i$: her payment). Values are independent private values: i.i.d. with CDF $F$ on $[0,1]$. Which of the following is common knowledge among the bidders?
options: The realized valuations $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_n$, but not the distribution $F$.
Both $F$ and all realized valuations, since the values are independent.
Neither $F$ nor the realized valuations; each bidder has her own view of $F$.
The distribution $F$ of valuations, but not the realized valuations.

questions.question: One object is sold to $n$ bidders; bidder $i$ privately knows her valuation $\theta_i$ and gets $\theta_i-p_i$ if she wins, $-p_i$ if she loses ($p_i$: her payment). Viewing the auction as a game with types, what is a pure strategy of bidder $i$?
options: A single bid $b_i\ge0$, chosen once she has learned the valuation she actually has.
A bidding function $b_i(\theta_i)$ that gives a bid for every possible valuation.
A bid $b_i(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_n)$ that depends on the valuations of all $n$ bidders.
A probability of winning that she chooses for each possible valuation $\theta_i$.

questions.question: One object is sold to $n$ bidders; bidder $i$ privately knows her valuation $\theta_i$ and gets $\theta_i-p_i$ if she wins, $-p_i$ if she loses ($p_i$: her payment). Values are private. Through which channel can a rival's valuation $\theta_j$ affect bidder $i$'s payoff?
options: Through $i$'s value: a high $\theta_j$ signals that the object is worth more to $i$ as well.
In no way: with private values the rivals' valuations never affect bidder $i$'s payoff.
Only through $i$'s payment; whether $i$ wins is decided by her own bid alone.
Only through the outcome: via $j$'s bid it affects whether $i$ wins and what she pays.

questions.question: One object is sold to $n$ bidders; bidder $i$ privately knows her valuation $\theta_i$ and gets $\theta_i-p_i$ if she wins, $-p_i$ if she loses ($p_i$: her payment). With $n=2$, bidder 1 ($\theta_1=0.8$) wins and pays $0.5$; bidder 2 ($\theta_2=0.6$) loses and pays $0$. What are the payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$?

One object is sold to $n$ bidders; bidder $i$ privately knows her valuation $\theta_i$ and gets $\theta_i-p_i$ if she wins, $-p_i$ if she loses ($p_i$: her payment). The rules make every bidder pay her own bid, and the highest bid wins. Bidder 1 has $\theta_1=0.6$, bids $0.2$ and loses. What is her payoff?

One object is sold to $n$ bidders; bidder $i$ privately knows her valuation $\theta_i$ and gets $\theta_i-p_i$ if she wins, $-p_i$ if she loses ($p_i$: her payment). Values are i.i.d. uniform on $[0,1]$, $n=3$, and all bidders use one common strictly increasing bidding function. What is the probability that a bidder with $\theta_i=0.6$ wins?

One object is sold to $n$ bidders; bidder $i$ privately knows her valuation $\theta_i$ and gets $\theta_i-p_i$ if she wins, $-p_i$ if she loses ($p_i$: her payment). A bidder with $\theta_i=0.7$ wins with probability $0.49$ and, when she wins, pays $0.4$; losers pay nothing. What is her interim expected payoff?

One object is sold to $n$ bidders; bidder $i$ privately knows her valuation $\theta_i$ and gets $\theta_i-p_i$ if she wins, $-p_i$ if she loses ($p_i$: her payment). With $n=2$, the rival's valuation is uniform on $[0,1]$, the rival bids $b(\theta)=\theta^2$, and the higher bid wins. With what probability does a bid of $0.36$ win?

One object is sold to $n$ bidders; bidder $i$ privately knows her valuation $\theta_i$ and gets $\theta_i-p_i$ if she wins, $-p_i$ if she loses ($p_i$: her payment). Bidders use bidding functions $b_j(\theta_j)$. What does a Bayesian Nash equilibrium require of bidder $i$'s bid when her valuation is $\theta_i$?
options: It gives her the best expected payoff against the rivals' bidding functions, averaging over their values.
It gives her the highest payoff against the rivals' realized bids, which she sees before bidding.
It gives her the highest probability of winning the object, whatever she has to pay.
It gives the highest total payoff of all bidders, since the allocation should be efficient.

questions.question: Two bidders privately observe $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$. Bidder 1's value for the object is $\tfrac{1}{2}(\theta_1+\theta_2)$. Is this a private-value setting for bidder 1?
options: Yes: she knows $\theta_1$, which is part of her value, so her value is private.
Yes: values are private as long as the signals $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ are independent.
No: learning $\theta_2$ would change her value, so it depends on the other's information.
No: a private value must be the same for both bidders, and here they may differ.

questions.question: One object is sold to $n$ bidders; bidder $i$ privately knows her valuation $\theta_i$ and gets $\theta_i-p_i$ if she wins, $-p_i$ if she loses ($p_i$: her payment). Values are independent private values: i.i.d. with CDF $F$ on $[0,1]$. Under which condition on the bidding functions does the object always go to a bidder with the highest valuation?
options: Each bidder uses some strictly increasing bidding function, possibly different.
All bidders use the same strictly increasing bidding function.
All bidders use the same bidding function, possibly flat in places.
Each bidder bids below her valuation, whatever the shape of her function.

questions.question: One object is sold to $n$ bidders; bidder $i$ privately knows her valuation $\theta_i$ and gets $\theta_i-p_i$ if she wins, $-p_i$ if she loses ($p_i$: her payment). Both bidders use $b(\theta)=\min(\theta,0.5)$, the higher bid wins and ties are broken by a fair coin. Valuations are $\theta_1=0.9$ and $\theta_2=0.7$. With what probability does the object go to the bidder with the lower valuation?

One object is sold to $n$ bidders; bidder $i$ privately knows her valuation $\theta_i$ and gets $\theta_i-p_i$ if she wins, $-p_i$ if she loses ($p_i$: her payment). Three bidders' values are i.i.d. with CDF $F(\theta)=\theta^3$ on $[0,1]$, and all use one common strictly increasing bidding function. Find the probability that a bidder with $\theta_i=0.8$ wins.

One object is sold to $n$ bidders; bidder $i$ privately knows her valuation $\theta_i$ and gets $\theta_i-p_i$ if she wins, $-p_i$ if she loses ($p_i$: her payment). Values are i.i.d. uniform on $[0,1]$, and in equilibrium a bidder of valuation $\theta$ has interim expected payoff $\theta^2/2$. What is her ex ante expected payoff, before she learns $\theta$?

Two bidders know their own values $\theta_1,\theta_2$, each depends only on its owner's taste, but the values are positively correlated (people with similar tastes bid). Which classification is correct?
options: Independent private values, since each value depends only on its owner.
Private values, but not independent private values.
Not private values, since correlation makes one value informative about the other.
Neither private nor independent, since the values are not known to the rival.

questions.question: One object is sold to $n$ bidders; bidder $i$ privately knows her valuation $\theta_i$ and gets $\theta_i-p_i$ if she wins, $-p_i$ if she loses ($p_i$: her payment). A student checks a proposed symmetric bidding function only at her own realized valuation $\theta_i=0.6$ and finds that the prescribed bid is optimal there. Why does this not establish an equilibrium?
options: It does establish one: only the realized valuation is relevant for her payoff.
Every valuation's bid must be optimal, since rivals face every possible valuation of hers.
Optimality must also hold at the rivals' realized valuations, which she cannot observe.
Optimality must hold on average over valuations, not at each separate valuation.

questions.question: One object is sold to $n$ bidders; bidder $i$ privately knows her valuation $\theta_i$ and gets $\theta_i-p_i$ if she wins, $-p_i$ if she loses ($p_i$: her payment). With $n=2$, every bidder pays her own bid and the higher bid wins. The rival's valuation is uniform on $[0,1]$ and she bids $\theta^2/2$. What is the expected payoff of a bidder with $\theta_i=0.8$ who bids $0.18$?

One object is sold to $n$ bidders; bidder $i$ privately knows her valuation $\theta_i$ and gets $\theta_i-p_i$ if she wins, $-p_i$ if she loses ($p_i$: her payment). With $n=2$, valuations are independent and uniform on $[0,1]$, bidder 1 bids $\theta_1/2$, bidder 2 bids $\theta_2$, and the higher bid wins. What is the probability that the object goes to the bidder with the lower valuation?
